opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and we talked about it a lot internally. The way I see it, "run at home" isn't really the only goal. When you release a very large model, the first audience isn't necessarily the hobbyist with a single GPU. It's researchers, startups, and companies who can afford some serious hardware or rent it in the cloud, and for them, having access to the weights of a frontier-level model is a big deal. They can study it, fine-tune it, and build on it in ways they never could with a closed API.

There's also a second-order effect that I think people underestimate. A big open model is a great teacher. You can use it to generate synthetic data, to distill into smaller models, to act as a judge or a reward model. So even if you can't run the largest model on your laptop, the smaller models you *do* run at home can end up much better because the big one exists and is open. The capability trickles down.

And then there's the community. Every time we've released something, people have been incredibly fast at quantizing it, optimizing inference, and finding ways to squeeze it onto hardware we didn't think was possible. So "can't run it at home" is often true on day one and much less true a few months later. Hardware keeps improving too.

So for me it's less about whether everyone can run it immediately, and more about pushing the frontier of what's available openly. If the best models are only behind closed doors, the whole ecosystem moves slower. Putting a really strong model out there raises the floor for everybody, even if not everybody is running that exact checkpoint.

r001.rationale: The response says the community quickly quantizes and optimizes inference to fit the model onto hardware, so it may be too large to run at home initially but become runnable later.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was a real debate internally when we did Llama 3, and especially with the 405B. There's a legitimate question: what's the point of open-sourcing a model that almost nobody can run on their own hardware? Most people doing fine-tuning or hobby projects are working with 8B, maybe 70B. The 405B needs a serious cluster just for inference.

But I think the framing of "run at home" is a bit misleading about what open source is for. Open source isn't only about individual developers on a laptop. It's about the ecosystem. The 405B is useful in a few ways that have nothing to do with running it yourself.

First, distillation. A frontier-level open model means anyone can generate synthetic data from it, do rejection sampling, and train smaller models. Before that, if you wanted GPT-4-level data you had to go through a closed API, with terms of service that usually forbid training on the outputs. With Llama you can. And that's genuinely how a lot of the 8B and 70B quality came about: we used the bigger models to improve the smaller ones. Making that available to the community lets them do the same.

Second, there's the research angle. If you want to study what happens at frontier scale, interpretability, safety, scaling behaviors, you need the weights. And people who can't run it themselves still benefit, because a few labs or universities with compute will do that work and publish it.

Third, the cloud providers. Everybody can run it through Together, Fireworks, AWS, whoever. The weights being open means there's competition on serving, prices come down, and you're not locked into one vendor. That's a very different situation from a single company controlling the API.

And then there's just the trajectory. The 405B is hard to run today. In a year or two, with quantization, better inference stacks, cheaper hardware, it won't be. We've seen this with every generation. The 70B felt enormous when Llama 2 came out, now people run it on a Mac. So releasing at the frontier is partly a bet on where hardware goes.

The last thing I'd say is, if we only released small models, we'd be implicitly agreeing that open source is for toys and closed models are for serious work. I don't believe that. The whole point was to show open can be at parity with the best closed models. You can't make that argument with an 8B.

r001.rationale: The response says quantization and better inference stacks may eventually make the 405B runnable on personal hardware, but it does not explain that open-sourcing enables community innovations that achieve this.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between open source and being able to run the model at home. Those are related, but they’re not the same thing. You can have a model that requires substantial infrastructure and still give people access to the weights, the ability to modify it, fine-tune it, and build on top of it.

And what people can run changes. The community finds ways to quantize models, make inference more efficient, and distill capabilities into smaller models. So I don’t think we should limit what we release to what fits on a consumer GPU today. Release the strongest model you can, and let people explore what they can do with it. Smaller, accessible models are important too; these are complementary goals.

r001.rationale: The response says the community can quantize models, improve inference efficiency, and distill capabilities into smaller models, allowing what people can run on consumer hardware to change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different things: being able to run the model at home, and having access to the model so you can build on it. Of course, if you release a very large model, not everyone has the hardware to run it. But people can use it to generate data, distill it into smaller models, quantize it, and find ways to make it more efficient. That’s part of what opening the model enables.

So I wouldn’t say we should wait until everyone can run it on a laptop. You release it, and then the community can work on making that capability more accessible. The large model can be useful directly, but it can also help improve the smaller models that people do run at home.

r001.rationale: It says releasing the large model lets the community find ways to make it more efficient and accessible, including quantization, so more people can run it at home.
